title: Chatbots and Checking Answers
learningIntention: I can explain how a chatbot makes text, give a reason it can be wrong, and check a reply against a trusted source.
teacherIntroduction: A chatbot is a computer program that writes a reply in everyday language. Today we will use a simple, unplugged model of how it makes text, look at why a fluent reply can still be wrong, and check prepared replies against a teacher-provided fact card. We will not create accounts, and we will not type personal information into a chatbot.
childActivity: Use teacher-prepared prompt and reply cards, check each reply against a fact card, write a short user story and two design criteria, then judge the fictional chatbot and suggest one change.
reflectionPrompt: What is one way you can check a chatbot reply before you rely on it?
movementMoment: Stand in two zones — Checked against the fact card, or Not yet checked — while you hold up one reply card, then sit and write your check.
stoppingPoint: We stop after checking the prepared replies and judging the fictional chatbot against the criteria. We do not create accounts or type personal information into a chatbot.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can say how the chatbot makes text, give one reason a reply can be wrong, and check a reply against the fact card. Do not collect names or personal data.
bestFit: A short Years 5–8 Digital Technologies mini-lesson on chatbots, run unplugged with prepared cards. No student accounts or live chatbot use is required.

title: Feeds and Recommendations
learningIntention: I can design a simple rule for choosing items in a feed and say whether the data a recommendation system collects is essential to its purpose.
teacherIntroduction: A feed is a list of posts or videos chosen for a person. A recommendation system uses data about what has been watched or tapped, then follows rules to choose what to show next. Today we will design a simple rule with branching and a repeat, and we will sort invented data items into essential and not essential. We will use a fictional feed only. We will not log in, and we will not inspect anyone’s real feed or digital footprint.
childActivity: Design a simple branching recommendation rule on paper, use it to fill a short fictional feed, then sort invented data items into Essential to the purpose and Not essential.
reflectionPrompt: Which data item was not essential to choosing the next video, and why?
movementMoment: Stand in two zones — Essential to the purpose, or Not essential — while you hold one invented data card, then sit and write a reason.
stoppingPoint: We stop after designing the rule and sorting the invented data items. We do not log in or look at anyone’s real feed or digital footprint.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can describe a branching rule, fill a short feed by repeating it, and say whether an invented data item is essential to the purpose. Do not collect names or personal data.
bestFit: A short Years 5–8 Digital Technologies mini-lesson on recommendation systems, run unplugged with a fictional feed. No student accounts.

title: Loot Boxes and In-game Purchases
learningIntention: I can explain that a loot box is a chance purchase, interpret a simple tally of results, and evaluate a fictional game’s design against agreed tests.
teacherIntroduction: A loot box is a purchase in a game that gives a chance item. You pay, or spend in-game currency, then chance decides what you get. You might not get the item you wanted, and some designs make it easy to try again. Today we will use a fair, unplugged chance model with teacher-prepared cards, record a class tally, and evaluate a fictional game against a user story and design criteria. We will not ask about anyone’s real spending or the games they play at home.
childActivity: Draw from a set of ten teacher-prepared cards (one rare, nine common), record a class tally, write a user story and design criteria, then judge a fictional loot-box design and suggest one change.
reflectionPrompt: What is one design choice that would make the chance clearer before someone spends?
movementMoment: After the first draw, stand in two zones — Common item, or Rare item — then sit and add your result to the class tally.
stoppingPoint: We stop after the tally and the evaluation of the fictional game. We do not ask about real spending, payment details, or games students play at home.
lightEvidence: Notice whether a student can explain that the item is decided by chance, use the class tally to support a statement, and judge the fictional design against a criterion. Do not collect names, spending details or personal data.
bestFit: A short Years 5–8 Digital Technologies mini-lesson on chance purchases in games, run unplugged with cards. No student accounts, and no discussion of real spending.
